content: Best Time to Visit |  Lorsch Abbey (© irish - Fotolia.com)  Introduction The former Imperial Abbey of Lorsch, 10 km east of Worms, was one of the most renowned monasteries of the Carolingian Empire. In 774, Charlemagne himself consecrated the abbey church, elevating Lorsch to the status of an imperial monastery under royal protection. Today, the surviving 9th-century gatehouse (Torhalle), portions of the basilica and sections of the surrounding wall stand as some of the finest pre-Romanesque remains north of the Alps and have been recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Interesting Facts about Lorsch Abbey  * **Lorsch Abbey** was founded in 764 by Count Cancor and his mother Williswinda, making it one of the earliest Carolingian monasteries in Germany. Today, only the magnificent Königshalle (King's Hall) remains largely intact as a testament to the abbey's former glory—this 9th-century gatehouse represents one of the finest examples of Carolingian architecture and earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 1991.

title: Lorsch Abbey and Lauresham
content: # Unesco Lorsch Abbey and Lauresham. Of the past and the future – the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Lorsch Abbey, with its adjoining open-air laboratory, is a living centre for research on the early Middle Ages. The UNESCO World Heritage Site of Lorsch Abbey – halfway between Darmstadt and Worms – is a place of concentrated cultural history. In 774, the ruler of an expanding great empire that laid the political and cultural foundations of Europe was even there in the flesh. Charles made Lorsch, blessed with the relics of Saint Nazarius, an imperial monastery, thus an agent of his politics, of a church reform and of educational programmes. At the same time, it is a place of work for scientists in a special field: They use experiments to question the past and (re)construct it. You can find event information and much more about Lorsch Abbey and the Lauresham Experimental Archaeological Open-Air Laboratory at www.kloster-lorsch.de.
